memories.memory_text: I called out to Adrian Adler from the kitchen, telling him breakfast was ready, but he didn’t answer—just kept on with that water-pick like I wasn’t even there. When he finally came in, he sat down and started eating without looking at me.

I asked if I could call him at the office, and he just stared at his food, asking why I’d want to. When he said he’d be out all day checking garages, I didn’t say anything—I just pushed my food around my plate. It felt like even wanting to reach out was wrong.
I heard a loud splash and some strange noise from the bathroom, so I poked my head around the corner—Adrian Adler was bent over, gripping his stomach like something was really wrong.
I asked if he was okay, but he didn’t answer—just kept brushing his teeth like I wasn’t even there, and after a while I sighed and walked away, feeling like he didn’t want me close.

I remember sitting on the sauna bench, the heat pressing down as Bennett Thorne leaned in and told me to get a doctor to see Adrian Adler without him knowing—her voice low and sure, like we were sharing a secret I wasn’t sure I wanted to keep. I just whispered, 'He'll be really mad,' feeling my chest tighten, but part of me wanted to do it, to finally know.

I said 'Excuse me, Wesley Sinclair. Gotta go,' when Evan Quincy called my name—my voice sounded shaky even to me, and I could feel my hands trembling as I stood up. I didn’t look back at Wesley Sinclair, just followed the doctor down the hall, my stomach tight with worry about what he might say about Adrian Adler’s condition.
I remember saying 'That's great, Doctor. Thanks,' after he finally agreed to come see Adrian Adler tonight—my hands were shaking a little, but I managed to smile and leave without looking back.
I picked up a few things from the shelves, but the thought of cooking or even eating made my stomach turn—I couldn't do it, so I just left with the magazine.
I walked down the Lakeview Station, knocked gently on Bennett Thorne's door, and let myself in—so quiet, so familiar, like I’ve done it a hundred times before.

Bennett Thorne looked up from her photos and told me to come back for dinner after Evan Quincy left, saying she’d be lonely if I didn’t — her voice was warm, insistent, like she really wanted me there.

I kept flipping through my Vogue, but I couldn’t focus—nothing held my attention, not even the clothes. I turned the the black letter on and cranked the volume up, just to fill the silence while I waited for Evan Quincy.

I was so tired, just waking up, and Adrian Adler’s voice kept calling me in that strange, wailing way—I couldn’t ignore it. When I sat beside him, he held me too tight and suddenly asked if I wanted to make love, saying I was the most sexy thing alive, over and over, like he wasn’t really seeing me.

I saw a black thread in the corner of Adrian Adler's mouth—like an insect's leg—and when I reached to brush it away, it twitched and pulled back inside. I yanked my hand away, covering my mouth, too terrified to breathe.

The thing came out more—Adrian Adler's lips parting like it was alive—and I couldn't stay. I don't remember getting up, but I was running, heart pounding, needing to get out before that thing fully emerged.
I ran down the Lakeview Station to Bennett Thorne's Eastgate Street, crying so hard I could barely see, my breath catching between sobs, and I didn’t stop—I just opened the door and went in.

I called out for Bennett Thorne, my voice trembling, and then saw her on the balcony—so still, her face painted in a way I didn’t recognize. When she turned and opened her arms, I froze for a second, unsure if this was really her.

I was sobbing in Bennett Thorne's lap, my face pressed against her thighs, and she was rocking me like I was a child, stroking my hair—her voice so calm, telling me not to worry, that everything was in the genes, and I felt so small, so soothed, whispering that she felt cosy, so cosy, like safety.

Bennett Thorne kissed me—soft at first, then her mouth wrenched open, her throat swelling grotesquely, and something alive forcing its way into my mouth; I gagged, tried to pull back, but her hands held me—cold, slick terror as it slithered down my throat.
I came up from the water, smiling—I felt so calm, like everything was finally right, and the others were there, watching me, waiting.
I kissed Evan Quincy under the water, holding his head tight—my throat swelled and something moved up from inside me, forcing its way into him, and I could feel it connecting us like iron.

memories.memory_text: I got two calls from Cameron Arden out of the blue—one to set up lunch, and then another to change the time. I didn’t think much of it then, but now it’s the only reason I was here.
I gestured for Spencer Rivers to follow me into my office, bypassing the others in the waiting room, including Wesley Sinclair who was mid-sentence with her.

I looked at Adrian Adler's file again after Spencer Rivers left, something in the numbers didn't add up—the cholesterol was low, blood pressure only slightly elevated, no signs of malignancy last year. I couldn't justify cancer progressing that fast, not like she described.

I asked Wesley Sinclair if the young woman he had contact with was from Eastgate Motel, and he confirmed she lived in unit 1208—my mind immediately went to the cluster of unexplained abdominal growths I’d seen in other patients from that building.

When I asked if her name was Robin Warren, and he said 'That's the one,' it hit me—she might be the common source, the first case I’ve been trying to trace through these patients with the strange abdominal lumps.

I was told I'm supposed to see Adrian Adler at ten, but I haven't arrived yet—Spencer Rivers just passed on the message while I was still at Bennett Thorne' Eastgate Street, surrounded by her photos and cluttered equipment on the walls.

Morgan Keaton dropped a stack of medical files and journals on my desk—Cameron Arden, Sidney Bellamy, the Bulletin of the Canadian Medical Association—stuff I’d asked for. I remember saying, 'That's great, Morgan Keaton, great. Thanks,' while already flipping through the papers.

While I was on the phone with Sidney Bellamy, I could see Morgan Keaton changing out of her nurse’s uniform in the corner—taking her time, not hiding it but not performing either. I kept one eye on her, one on Cameron Arden’s notes, while talking.
I didn't understand what Sidney Bellamy meant when he said Lane Sterling was 'a disease to save man from his mind'—it made no sense to me at first.

I was holding the Velakofsky file, looking at the X-rays of those dark, blurred masses in his abdomen, when I realized Morgan Keaton was getting dressed—she was leaving—and I told Sidney Bellamy that Cameron Arden might not have known, but Robin Warren had been with several men at Eastgate Motel, and now three or four of them had these unidentifiable growths.
I agreed to Morgan Keaton’s supper invitation, but only if it was late—after I met Sidney Bellamy at Adrian Adler’s. I needed to make it clear my work came first.
Morgan Keaton burst into my office, sobbing and barely able to speak—she’d been attacked, she said, by someone she knew, and she thought she’d killed him.
After holding her for a moment, I had to pull back and ask where the man was—I needed to see if he was still there, if this was really about the organism.

I saw the burn on Nico Langley's forearm right away—blistered, raw tissue from that creature's solvent. I told Morgan Keaton to take them back to 703 and treat it as best she could for now, second-degree, no delay.
After handing my bag to Morgan Keaton, I asked where the creature went—Spergazzi said he threw it down to the incinerator on his cane. I told Morgan Keaton I was going down there, and then I left.

I couldn't see inside the incinerator at first, so I looked around and spotted the superintendent's flashlight on top of a heating pipe—I took it down, turned it on, and went back to searching for the dead the leather badge.
I found Lane Sterling corpse in the incinerator, pulled it out with the poker, and held it up to the light—its insides glowed, twisted and alien, like something wasn't right about its structure.

A man came up behind me, grabbed me, and tried to kiss my neck—then my mouth—I fought back with the poker, hit him in the chest and ankle, and ended up kicking him in the head until he stopped moving.
I left the body near the incinerator door, blood pooling on the floor—I didn’t have time to move it further before Morgan Keaton came down.
I buzzed the Spergazzi Eastgate Street and asked to speak to the nurse, but Lane Vale said she had gone away—maybe to look for me—and in that moment, I knew something was wrong enough to act.
I saw bloodied handprints on the door to the garage as soon as I got down the stairs—someone had pressed hard, fingers smeared in panic.
When I opened the garage door, Morgan Keaton's screams came echoing out—sharp, desperate, and unmistakably hers.
I smashed the Graham Finch with his own gun, then fired three times into his upper body—he was covered in blood and drool, and I couldn't risk him hurting Morgan Keaton any longer.

I found Morgan Keaton in her the small badge with the Graham Finch on top of her. I took his gun and hit him with it, then shot him three times. I pulled him off her, got her into the passenger seat, and tried to drive out. A the small badge blocked the exit, so I swerved and hit a post. I got out, fired the gun at the Evan Grayson, one fell back and blocked the others, then I carried Morgan Keaton out.

I half-dragged Morgan Keaton down the Lakeview Station, moving past open doors where people were tangled together on floors and furniture, the air thick with moans and whispers—I just kept my head down and pushed forward.
I saw the exit door standing open ahead and rushed through it, pulling Morgan Keaton with me—finally out of that noise, out of those rooms.
I checked the gym carefully before pulling Morgan Keaton inside, then blocked the door with a box horse and a weight-lifting table so no one could get in easily.
I knelt beside Morgan Keaton as she started to come around, brushed the blood-matted hair from her face, and said Sidney Bellamy would be here soon—more to steady myself than to reassure her.

I was about to kiss her—she pulled me in close, whispering that strange dream about Freud, her voice so slow and steady it made my thoughts blur. Her lips were almost on mine when her mouth snapped open and I saw the tentacles moving inside.

I shoved a wad of cloth into her mouth and tied it shut with a strip from her blouse—she thrashed against me, moaning through the gag. Then I threw her over my shoulder and carried her out, her body writhing the whole way.

I held Morgan Keaton against the wall while blood poured from her mouth and something tore its way out through the gag—tentacles writhing, searching for grip. I let go, and she just sank to the floor.

From above, I looked down and saw a resident pull the thing from her mouth and swallow it whole. Others were touching her body—stroking, caressing—like it was some kind of ritual. I couldn't stay. I ran.

I was backing away from the pool when someone shoved me hard from behind—I couldn't catch myself, and I fell in, thrashing in the water. Bennett Thorne came at me fast and pinned me under the surface, holding me down while they all chanted.

Spencer Rivers kissed me underwater, but it wasn't human—her throat swelled and something forced its way into my mouth. I felt my own face bulge as tentacles pushed in, and I could taste blood as I struggled before going still.
I glanced into the rearview mirror and saw the lights of the other cars lined up behind me, all ready to move.
I smiled and stepped on the accelerator, feeling the the small badge surge forward as the others began to follow me onto the street.

memories.memory_text: I was cleaning my teeth with the water-pick, focusing on every detail, and when Spencer Rivers called about breakfast, I didn’t answer. I just kept going until it felt right.
I slid the key into Robin Warren's lock, turned it slow, then knocked—just once—before opening the door. I stepped in quiet and shut it behind me, not looking up, just hoping no one saw my face.

I smelled burned flesh the second I walked in, and I knew—something was wrong, something was so wrong. I saw Cameron Arden’s foot first, then her on the table, still smoking, eyes open, that clip still on her lips.
I felt it again near my navel—hard, familiar—like it was waiting for me, and I knew right away it hadn't gone away.
I doubled over silently, the water-pick thrashing in the sink, and I had to hide the pain when Spencer Rivers looked in—couldn't let her see.

I was on the floor, breathing heavily, and then Mrs. Wheatley was there, helping me up, leaning me on the desk. She used a Kleenex to wipe blood from the corner of my mouth and showed it to me, saying it was from inside me.
After she left, the pain came again, sharp in my gut, and I felt the blood seep out—I tasted it, metallic, and licked it off my lips without thinking.
I signed the chit, hands shaking, and stepped out of the cab—legs wobbling, like I might fall.
I walked in, and the Graham Finch opened the doors, said 'Afternoon, Adrian Adler'—I didn't look at him, just kept moving, but I felt it, the way he still called me 'Mr.' like I was still someone.
The doctor kept staring at my file, moving papers around, like he didn’t believe me. I could feel it—the doubt in the air, heavy, like it was pressing on my chest.

I was on the sofa, just trying to sit still, and then my body locked up—I couldn’t breathe, couldn’t speak—my hands flew to my mouth like something was going to come up, and I fell to the floor, twisting, unable to stop it.

I barely made it to the bathroom, threw myself over the tub, and gagged—something thick and wet tore out of me, streaked with blood—and then I just collapsed, spent, on the floor, my mouth tasting of iron.

I stumbled into the living room, my breath ragged, and sat facing the glass door—couldn't see straight, just kept gasping, muttering to myself like it would help. Then I got up, opened the door, and stepped onto the balcony, the cold air hitting my skin.

I was holding the railing, trying to breathe, and then my neck locked up—my mouth wrenched open, I couldn't stop it, my hands flew to my face but I couldn't hold it down, and I just started retching over the edge, gagging, moaning, I couldn't control any of it.
I tapped on my skin near the navel, whispering, 'Here, boy, here,' trying to coax it out again, and when I finally stroked the lump, it pulsed under my fingers like it was answering me.
When Spencer Rivers came in and tried to pull the covers off, I rolled away, hiding it—my stomach—and told her to go away, even though I saw her start to cry.
My name was called when Morgan Keaton handed over files to Evan Quincy. She said, 'Files on Horsefield, Adrian Adler, Swinburne, and Velakofsky,' and threw the papers onto the desk.
They’re meeting at my place, I heard Evan Quincy say it—Eastgate Street 1009, South Tower. I didn’t say yes, I didn’t agree, but they’re coming anyway.
I feel the lumps moving under my skin near my navel, shifting and pulsing, and my hands are pressed there like I'm holding something sacred inside me.
I'm making these soft, crooning sounds without meaning to, like a lullaby gone wrong, while the things inside me keep moving.

I called out to Spencer Rivers from the bed, my voice high and urgent, and when she came, I told her I felt wonderful—so wonderful—and I pulled her close, needing her to start, to begin, because I couldn’t remember how.

She touched my stomach and jerked her hand back like I was something broken—something wrong—and I didn’t understand, I only knew she had to keep going, had to love me, because she was my wife, she was my wife.
I wailed for Spencer Rivers, calling her name over and over, my voice tearing out of me like something not mine.
I felt my throat swelling, pulsing, and my lips twitching like I couldn't control them—something was moving inside me, forcing its way up.
I heard the knock, and then silence—another knock. I stayed still. Then the knob turned, and the door opened. I didn’t say come in. I didn’t say anything.

I was lying in bed, so weak, couldn't move or speak—just floating in and out, feeling the weight of my body but not in control. I heard a voice calling my name, but I couldn't answer, couldn't even close my mouth.

I felt the covers pulled back, cold air on my skin, and then—something moved inside me. I didn't see it, but I knew they were there, my blood, my life—I had to protect them. I couldn't let him hurt them.
